title: Adaptation
description: The adaptation exclusion, IRC § 41(d)(4)(B), bars credit claims for work that merely adapts an existing business component to a customer's requirement.
summary: The adaptation exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) bars U.S. taxpayers from claiming the federal research tax credit for work that merely adapts an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(3), customer-specific projects still qualify when they resolve technological uncertainty through a process of experimentation covering at least 80% of research activities.

body.text: The adaptation exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) bars U.S. taxpayers from claiming the federal research tax credit for work that merely adapts an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(3), customer-specific projects still qualify when they resolve technological uncertainty through a process of experimentation covering at least 80% of research activities.

The Adaptation Exclusion under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41(d)(4)(B) (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(B)) bars from qualified research any activities related to adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need. Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3) mitigates that statutory prohibition by clarifying that the exclusion does not apply merely because a business component is intended for a specific customer. Furthermore, in the preamble to Treasury Decision 9104 (T.D. 9104, issued January 2, 2004), the Treasury Department and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) stated their interpretive view that the adaptation exclusion does not disqualify research activities that otherwise satisfy the statutory four-part test for qualified research under IRC § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a). Consequently, custom manufacturing, contract engineering, and bespoke software development projects remain eligible for the federal Research Credit if the taxpayer substantiates that the work sought to discover technological information to resolve uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design at the outset of the project through a qualifying process of experimentation covering at least 80% of the business component's research activities.

Specifically, primary extraction of Title 26 of the United States Code confirms both the exact subparagraph designation 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(B) for the adaptation exclusion and the verbatim six-category definition of a "business component" in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(B) (any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business).

Both the general IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 — Qualified Research Activities (published June 2005, republished 2008, webpage updated July 2, 2026) and the IRS Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software (updated June 8, 2026) contain dedicated subsections titled "Exclusion for Adaptation". Whereas the general ATG cites 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Examples 3–7 as illustrating the adaptation exclusion, the software audit guidelines specifically cite Examples 3 and 7. Primary regulatory text confirms that within 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Examples 3, 4, and 5 address adapting a core general ledger accounting software program to a specific customer's requirements (evaluating vendor in-house expenses, customer contract research payments, and customer in-house employee wages); Example 6 (rather than Example 3) is the passenger rail car illustration where a customer orders fewer seats and commercially available upgraded seating material and carpet; and Example 7 illustrates how a valve manufacturer overcomes the adaptation exclusion when modifying preexisting robotic equipment through modeling, simulation, and extensive scientific and laboratory testing to resolve technological uncertainty.

Under LB&I-04-0125-0001 (dated January 3, 2025) and Taxpayer Services interim guidance TS-21-0126-0032 (dated January 2, 2026), the IRS waived two of the five upfront refund-claim filing items (individual performer names and the specific information each individual sought to discover) for claims postmarked on or after June 18, 2024, and extended the 45-day perfection transition period through January 10, 2027.
Statutory and Regulatory Framework for the Adaptation Exclusion
Statutory Boundary Under IRC Section 41

The statutory exclusion for adaptation is codified in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(B) (IRC § 41(d)(4)(B)). Within the statutory structure of IRC § 41(d), paragraph (1) establishes four cumulative requirements that research activities must satisfy to constitute "qualified research":

items: The Section 174 Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)): The research must be activity with respect to which expenditures may be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174 (reflecting the conforming amendment enacted by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, Pub. L. 115-97, § 13206(d)(1), which substituted "specified research or experimental expenditures under section 174" for "expenses under section 174").
The Technological Information Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i)): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information which is technological in nature.

The Business Component Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii)): The application of that technological information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer.

The Process of Experimentation and Qualified Purpose Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and § 41(d)(3)(A)): Substantially all of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality.

body.text: Even where a taxpayer's activities involve engineering or software development, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4) ("Activities for which credit not allowed") carves out eight express statutory exclusions (subparagraphs (A) through (H)): (A) research conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component; (B) adaptation of existing business components; (C) duplication of an existing business component from physical examination, plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information; (D) efficiency surveys, management functions or techniques, market research, testing, or development, routine data collection, or routine testing or inspection for quality control; (E) computer software developed by or for the benefit of the taxpayer primarily for internal use (except as provided in regulations or for use in qualified research or a qualifying production process); (F) foreign research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States; (G) research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities; and (H) research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity. Subparagraph (B) states verbatim:
(B) Adaptation of existing business components.—Any research related to the adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need.

Deconstructing the statutory text of IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) reveals three threshold elements that trigger the exclusion: first, the activity must involve research or modification activity; second, its object must be an existing business component (rather than the creation of a fundamentally new business component); and third, the modification must be undertaken to adapt that existing component to a particular customer's requirement or need.

Crucially, there has been a long-standing doctrinal tension between the legislative history of the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (Pub. L. 99-514, § 231(b)) and subsequent Treasury regulatory interpretation regarding whether IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) operates independently of the four-part test in IRC § 41(d)(1). As noted in professional tax commentary (The Tax Adviser, June 2024), the House Conference Report on the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (H.R. Conf. Rep. No. 99-841) suggested that Congress intended the IRC § 41(d)(4) exclusions—including the adaptation exclusion—to apply independently of whether the underlying activities met IRC § 41(d)(1). However, when promulgating final regulations in T.D. 9104 (January 2, 2004), the Treasury Department and the IRS expressly rejected an independent, mechanical application of the exclusion, stating in the regulatory preamble that the exclusions for research after commercial production, adaptation of existing business components, and duplication of existing business components "do not cover research activities that otherwise satisfy the requirements for qualified research".

Federal jurisprudence confirms that courts evaluate the IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) adaptation exclusion in close tandem with the IRC § 174 and IRC § 41(d)(1) uncertainty and experimentation tests. In Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, the U.S. Tax Court examined research credit claims by shareholders of Catalytic Products International Inc. (CPI), an S corporation that designed and supplied custom-built catalytic and thermal oxidizers (air pollution control systems) tailored to customer specifications. The Tax Court disallowed the credits because CPI's development costs failed the IRC § 174 uncertainty test incorporated via IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)—finding that CPI's engineers had sufficient information at the outset to establish appropriate designs using standardized proposal spreadsheets prior to production—and because certain contracts constituted excluded funded research under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H). Addressing IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) specifically in connection with CPI's M&W Ireland project (Project No. 14-07718), the Tax Court held in a footnote that where the contract required CPI to deliver an exact copy of a previously supplied wastewater treatment system with only minor, site-specific modifications to comply with European standards, the expenditures were barred under the plain meaning of the adaptation exclusion. In reaching this conclusion, Betz cited Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States, 691 F. Supp. 688, 697 n.11 (N.D. Tex. 2010), which held that the adaptation exclusion applies to a taxpayer's refinement of a preliminary design provided by a customer, alongside earlier precedent in Eustace v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2001-66, aff'd, 312 F.3d 905 (7th Cir. 2002), and Davenport v. Commissioner, 897 F. Supp. 2d 496.
Regulatory Mitigation Under Treas. Reg. Section 1.41-4(c)(3)

Without regulatory clarification, a literal reading of IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) could threaten to disqualify substantial volumes of contract engineering, custom equipment fabrication, and bespoke enterprise software development performed under customer contracts. Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3)—which forms part of 26 CFR § 1.41-4, governing qualified research for expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003, and remaining current in the Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (eCFR) as of November 9, 2026—establishes the operative boundary in two concise sentences:

(3) Adaptation of existing business components. Activities relating to adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need are not qualified research. This exclusion does not apply merely because a business component is intended for a specific customer.

Promulgated in final form by T.D. 9104 on January 2, 2004 (2004-6 I.R.B., following earlier proposed regulations REG-105170-97 on December 2, 1998, final regulations T.D. 8930 on January 3, 2001, Notice 2001-19, and reproposed regulations REG-112991-01 on December 26, 2001), 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3) was retained intact while Treasury revised the process of experimentation, shrinking-back, and illustrative example provisions of § 1.41-4. Both the general IRS Research Credit ATG and the IRS Software Process of Experimentation Audit Guidelines repeat the regulatory rule verbatim, adding a third sentence regarding third-party contractors: "A contractor's adaptation of an existing business component to a taxpayer's particular requirement or need is not qualified research."

Legally and operationally, the second sentence of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3)—reinforced by the T.D. 9104 preamble—shifts the compliance inquiry away from the commercial trigger (whether the project was initiated by a single customer's purchase order or contract) and toward the technical nature of the development work. Designing a custom airframe sub-assembly, formulating a novel high-temperature polymer for a single industrial buyer, or architecting a bespoke real-time data synchronization engine for a specific enterprise client is not disqualified by IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) if the underlying activities satisfy all elements of IRC § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a) and are not otherwise excluded as funded research under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(9) (which cross-references 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)).
Existing Business Components and the Shrinking-Back Rule

Because the adaptation exclusion applies specifically to the adaptation of an "existing business component," accurate application of the rule depends on the statutory definition of a business component and the regulatory mechanics of the shrinking-back rule. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A), the qualification tests of IRC § 41(d)(1) must be applied separately with respect to each business component of the taxpayer. Subparagraph 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(B) defines a "business component" in six specific statutory categories:

(B) Business component defined.—The term "business component" means any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be— (i) held for sale, lease, or license, or (ii) used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer.

In addition, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C) establishes a special statutory rule for production processes: "Any plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production of a business component shall be treated as a separate business component (and not as part of the business component being produced)." Implementing this rule, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(1) mandates that research activities relating to the development of a manufacturing or commercial production process are not qualified research unless the requirements of IRC § 41(d) and § 1.41-4 are satisfied independently for the process without taking into account research activities relating to the product itself (and vice versa).

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2), the evaluation does not jump directly to the "smallest" subset; rather, it proceeds sequentially top-down from the discrete business component to the most significant subset of elements:

(2) Shrinking-back rule. The requirements of section 41(d) and paragraph (a) of this section are to be applied first at the level of the discrete business component, that is, the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. If these requirements are not met at that level, then they apply at the most significant subset of elements of the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license. This shrinking back of the product is to continue until either a subset of elements of the product that satisfies the requirements is reached, or the most basic element of the product is reached and such element fails to satisfy the test. This shrinking-back rule is applied only if a taxpayer does not satisfy the requirements of section 41(d)(1) and paragraph (a)(2) of this section with respect to the overall business component. The shrinking-back rule is not itself applied as a reason to exclude research activities from credit eligibility.

The final two sentences of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)—added in T.D. 9104 in response to taxpayer comments that the 2001 proposed regulations implied shrinking back could be used to carve out and disallow portions of an otherwise qualifying component—are critical: the shrinking-back rule applies only when the overall business component fails IRC § 41(d)(1) and § 1.41-4(a)(2), and cannot be wielded by examiners as an independent basis to exclude research activities from credit eligibility.

Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(3) illustrates this sequential top-down mechanism: when X, a motorcycle engine builder, develops a new carburetor and modifies an existing motorcycle engine design to accommodate the new carburetor, the requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1) and § 1.41-4(a) are applied first to the overall motorcycle engine. If the modifications to the engine as a whole (including the carburetor development) do not satisfy IRC § 41(d)(1) and § 1.41-4(a)—for instance, because the engine modifications are minor adaptations or fail the 80% process of experimentation threshold—those requirements are then applied to the next most significant subset of elements of the business component. Assuming the carburetor is the next most significant subset, the research activities incurred in developing the new carburetor independently constitute qualified research if they satisfy IRC § 41(d)(1) and § 1.41-4(a).

In the specific context of the adaptation exclusion, the preamble to T.D. 9104 explicitly instructs taxpayers to review activities that might otherwise appear to fall within the adaptation exclusion by applying the shrinking-back rule so that eligible subcomponents and subsystems are properly isolated and included in credit computations. However, judicial decisions in Betz v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2023-84), Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023)), and Suder v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2014-201) underscore a strict evidentiary prerequisite: a taxpayer cannot invoke 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) at trial or audit unless its project accounting and technical records allow the court or the IRS to identify the specific subcomponent and quantify the specific hours, wages, and supply expenses devoted to that qualifying subset. In Betz, although the Tax Court acknowledged that certain pilot-model wages and supplies might theoretically qualify at the component or subcomponent level via shrinking back under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2), the court denied relief because the taxpayer failed to introduce subcomponent-level documentation and time tracking.
Adaptation Exclusion Versus the Process of Experimentation
Technological Uncertainty and the 80 Percent Substantially All Rule

In both IRS examination practice and Tax Court litigation, the adaptation exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3) operates as the doctrinal counterpart to the technological uncertainty and Process of Experimentation (PoE) requirements under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)–(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)–(6). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature only if it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component. Regulatory uncertainty exists strictly when the information available to the taxpayer "does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of the business component."

Paragraph (a)(3)(ii) clarifies that a taxpayer is not required to seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the relevant field of science or engineering, nor must the research succeed in developing the new or improved business component. Paragraph (a)(3)(iii) establishes the patent safe harbor: the issuance of a utility patent by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office under 35 U.S.C. § 151 (other than a design patent issued under 35 U.S.C. § 171) is conclusive evidence that the taxpayer discovered technological information intended to eliminate uncertainty, though obtaining a patent is not a precondition for claiming the credit. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4), the process used to discover such information is technological in nature if it fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science, and taxpayers may employ existing technologies and rely on existing scientific or engineering principles to satisfy this test. Simultaneously, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(7) cautions that the mere employment of computers or information technology—or reliance on computer science principles to store, collect, manipulate, translate, disseminate, produce, distribute, or process data—does not by itself establish that qualified research has been undertaken.
To defeat an IRS assertion that customer-specific work is non-qualified adaptation, the taxpayer must satisfy 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), which defines a process of experimentation as:

... a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities. A process of experimentation must fundamentally rely on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science and involves the identification of uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component, the identification of one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty, and the identification and the conduct of a process of evaluating the alternatives (through, for example, modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial and error methodology). A process of experimentation must be an evaluative process and generally should be capable of evaluating more than one alternative. A taxpayer may undertake a process of experimentation if there is no uncertainty concerning the taxpayer's capability or method of achieving the desired result so long as the appropriate design of the desired result is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities.

As emphasized in Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), and reiterated by the Seventh Circuit in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), a qualifying process of experimentation "must involve a methodical plan involving a series of trials to test a hypothesis, analyze the data, refine the hypothesis, and retest the hypothesis so that it constitutes experimentation in the scientific sense." Merely demonstrating that design uncertainty existed at the outset of a customer contract and was ultimately eliminated by delivering a working product is legally insufficient without proof of the structured, scientific evaluation of alternatives.

(6) Substantially all requirement. In order for activities to constitute qualified research under section 41(d)(1), substantially all of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation that relates to a qualified purpose. The substantially all requirement of section 41(d)(1)(C) and paragraph (a)(2)(iii) of this section is satisfied only if 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (and without regard to section 1.41-2(d)(2)), constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a purpose described in section 41(d)(3). Accordingly, if 80 percent (or more) of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to a business component constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a purpose described in section 41(d)(3), the substantially all requirement is satisfied even if the remaining 20 percent (or less) of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to the business component do not constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a purpose described in section 41(d)(3), so long as these remaining research activities satisfy the requirements of section 41(d)(1)(A) and are not otherwise excluded under section 41(d)(4). The substantially all requirement is applied separately to each business component.

The decision in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023)—which is also cited on page 14 of IRS Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F—illustrates how the 80% rule governs custom, first-in-class manufacturing and engineering projects. In Little Sandy Coal, the taxpayer's shipbuilding subsidiary contracted with customers to design, fabricate, and deliver a custom tanker barge and a floating dry dock, claiming the vessels as first-in-class "pilot models" under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(4). Both the Tax Court and the Seventh Circuit rejected the "feels new enough" novelty shortcut previously applied in Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States, 691 F. Supp. 688, 694 (N.D. Tex. 2010), holding that the novelty of a custom-built product is not a "consistently applied reasonable basis" for measuring the 80% fraction under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6). Specifically, the Seventh Circuit held that the "substantially all" fraction (research activities that constitute elements of a process of experimentation divided by total research activities) must be substantiated activity by activity for each business component, that direct supervision and support activities that are not themselves elements of a process of experimentation cannot be assumed into the numerator without rigorous proof, and that labeling a custom customer deliverable a "pilot model" does not carry the whole unit through the 80% test. Because the shipbuilder relied on generalized trial testimony rather than contemporaneous time or cost accounting showing that at least 80% of the vessel research activities constituted elements of a process of experimentation, the entire credit was disallowed.

Finally, the IRS Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software (updated June 8, 2026) explicitly distinguish qualifying technological (software development) uncertainty from non-qualifying business and project management uncertainties. The IRS guidelines observe that software projects frequently fail or encounter difficulties due to business or project management factors rather than technical uncertainty, enumerating nine common non-technical failure factors:

items: Incomplete and/or changing user requirements;
Lack of user involvement;
Lack of resources (budget or staffing);
Unrealistic expectations;
Lack of executive support;
Lack of planning;
Commercial obsolescence ("didn't need it any longer");
Lack of IT management; and
Technological illiteracy.

body.text: Similarly, when evaluating Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs), the IRS software audit guidelines classify decisions regarding what data items and graphics should be displayed on a screen, and where on each screen each item should be placed, as business and/or project uncertainties rather than technological uncertainties resolved through a process of experimentation.
Routine Customer Modifications and Excluded Activities

Separating primary statutory and regulatory authorities from secondary tax-consultancy commentary clarifies which customer-driven modifications fail to qualify as research under IRC § 41(d). First, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), any research related to "style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors" is statutorily barred from constituting a qualified purpose. Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 1 illustrates that when widget manufacturer X obtains sample shades of green paint and surveys customers to change a widget's color from blue to green, the activities are excluded because they relate to style, taste, or cosmetic factors. In Example 2 of § 1.41-4(a)(8), when X modifies its painting process to accommodate the chosen green paint by consulting its spray-machine manufacturer—who instructs X to acquire a specific nozzle—and X tests the nozzles to verify they work as specified, X has not conducted a process of experimentation because the equipment vendor eliminated the technical uncertainty, and X's testing is routine quality control under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(v).

Second, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Examples 3, 4, and 5 address adapting a core software program across vendor, contract, and in-house customer arrangements. In Example 3 (Software Vendor's In-House Adaptation), X, a computer software development firm, owns all substantial rights in a general ledger accounting software core program that X markets and licenses to customers, and incurs expenditures in adapting the core software program to the unique requirements of C, one of X's customers; because X's activities represent activities to adapt an existing software program to a particular customer's requirement or need, they are excluded from qualified research under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3). In Example 4 (Customer's Contract Research Payments), assuming the same facts as Example 3 except that customer C pays vendor X to adapt the core software program to C's requirements, C's payments to X are not for qualified research under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3) and therefore do not qualify as contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A). In Example 5 (Customer's In-House Employee Wages), assuming the same facts as Example 3 except that customer C's own employees adapt the licensed core software program to C's requirements, C's employee activities are excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3), and the wages C paid to its employees do not constitute in-house research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A).

Third, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 6 and Example 7 contrast non-qualified manufacturing adaptation with qualified experimental modification of existing equipment. In Example 6 (Custom Passenger Rail Car Configuration), manufacturer X produces and sells rail cars whose designs are ordinarily subject to extensive, complex scientific and laboratory testing due to strict performance, reliability, and quality specifications. Customer B orders passenger rail cars from X with requirements differing from X's existing models solely in that B wants fewer seats and commercially available higher-quality seating material and carpet. Example 6 concludes that the rail car sold to B was not a new business component, but merely an adaptation of an existing business component that did not require a process of experimentation; thus, X's manufacturing activities for B are excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3). (Note: Prior secondary summaries occasionally misattributed this passenger rail car illustration to Example 3, which in the Code of Federal Regulations is the general ledger software adaptation example.) Conversely, in Example 7 (Experimental Modification of Existing Equipment Overcoming Adaptation), manufacturer X undertakes to create a manufacturing process for a new valve design requiring specialized robotic equipment that is not commercially available. X purchases preexisting robotic equipment to modify it for its valve process, and X's engineers identify technological uncertainty concerning how to modify the equipment. The engineers develop several alternative designs, conduct experiments using modeling and simulation, and perform extensive scientific and laboratory testing of design alternatives before constructing and installing the modified robotic equipment. Example 7 concludes that X's research activities to determine how to modify the purchased robotic equipment are not excluded under the adaptation exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3).

Fourth, under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), evaluating commercial warehouse management software products from marketplace vendors (Example 5) or evaluating standard ERP templates, reports, and routine data transfer scripts (Example 9) does not constitute a process of experimentation. By contrast, conducting systematic trial-and-error testing of newly designed data caching and synchronization algorithms to eliminate data synchronization uncertainty between a legacy system and an ERP system (Example 10) does constitute elements of a qualifying process of experimentation.

Fifth, while secondary articles often use the shorthand phrase "adaptive maintenance", the IRS Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software (updated June 8, 2026) directly reference the IEEE Standard for Software Maintenance, Software Engineering Standards Committee of the IEEE Computer Society, June 25, 1998, pages 3 & 4, and classify software activities into High Risk (usually fail IRC § 41(d)), Moderate Risk (often fail), and Low Risk (rarely fail). Under the IRS guidelines, five major customization and maintenance categories are rated High Risk or generally non-qualifying:

items: Software Application Configuration: Configuring purchased vendor applications (such as defining charts of accounts, defining user counts, setting report access privileges, selecting among vendor-defined options, or modifying default capabilities using vendor-provided software).

Modifying Existing Software for New Devices, Standards, or Vendor Platform Certification: Examining existing code or documentation, reverse engineering, debugging, and running target vendor validation or certification test suites to verify that software works according to standards or devices.

Vendor Product Extensions: Writing customer code via well-defined vendor interfaces ("user exits") or Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) to fill functional gaps—such as custom spreadsheet calculations or custom report formats—where the vendor's core product is unmodified and the new code simply conforms to the vendor's API.

Interface Software Development and Routine Data Conversion: Defining data and transaction requirements to connect internal or external applications or adding a web browser interface (Interface software development), as well as extracting data from a hierarchical database, converting data formats, and loading it into a relational database (Data conversion).

Reverse Engineering: Examining existing programs, databases, and files to determine how a legacy application or interface operates (explicitly excluded under IRC § 41(d) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 8).

body.text: While doctrinally consistent with 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3) and (c)(3)—because applying known methods and familiar materials involves no technological uncertainty—practitioners should cite primary authorities (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Examples 3–6, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Examples 1–2, 5, 9, and Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84) rather than treating consultancy bullet points as official IRS ATG text.
Comparative Criteria and the Qualification Matrix

cells: Controlling Legal Authority
Underlying Technical Objective
Tailoring, configuring, or resizing an existing business component to meet a specific customer's specification or site requirement using established capabilities and known engineering methods.

Discovering technological information intended to eliminate uncertainty in developing a new or improved business component (or qualifying subset under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)) for improved function, performance, reliability, or quality.
Nature of Uncertainty at Inception

Absent, resolved by an outside equipment/software vendor (§ 1.41-4(a)(8), Ex. 2), or limited to cosmetic/style factors (§ 41(d)(3)(B)), software configuration, API extensions, or business/project management uncertainties.

Information available to the taxpayer at the outset does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the component, or the appropriate design of the component (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i)).
Evaluative Process and Quantitative Floor

Linear engineering implementation, spreadsheet design finalization prior to production (Betz), routine data conversion, vendor certification testing, or experimentation covering less than 80% of component research activities (Little Sandy Coal).

Methodical evaluation of alternatives via modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error fundamentally relying on physical/biological sciences, engineering, or computer science across 80% or more of the component's research activities (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)).
Audit and Judicial Substantiation Burden
Defaults to disallowance where the taxpayer demonstrates only a finished customer deliverable, relies on "first-in-class" novelty shortcuts, or provides uncorroborated oral testimony.

Taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of proof to substantiate initial technical uncertainty, hypotheses and alternatives evaluated, and the 80% PoE fraction at the component or shrunk-back subcomponent level ("walk by sight, not by faith").

body.text: Second, labeling the X-axis "Technological Uncertainty (Risk of Failure)" requires nuance: while economic risk of failure is relevant to whether research is "funded" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1) (whether payment is contingent on the success of the research), technological uncertainty under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) and (a)(5)(i) exists even when the taxpayer has no uncertainty regarding its ultimate capability or method of achieving the result, so long as the appropriate design of that result is uncertain at the outset. Moreover, under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), a taxpayer need not succeed (or fail) in developing the component to qualify. Third, the only binding numerical threshold in Treasury regulations is the 80% or more "substantially all" requirement under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), which measures the proportion of a business component's research activities (on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis) that constitute elements of a process of experimentation.
Hypothetical Software and Manufacturing Scenarios

cells: Enterprise Software Scenario 1 (Taxpayer Z / Customer A)

Taxpayer Z licenses proprietary inventory software and contracts with Customer A to reorder input screen fields and reconfigure standard reports for client cost centers using known programming and SQL queries.
Excluded Adaptation.

Excluded: Directly analogous to 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Examples 3–5 (adapting core accounting software to customer C's requirements) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 9 (standard ERP templates/reports). Also classified as High Risk under the IRS Software PoE Audit Guidelines (Software application configuration, Vendor product extensions, and GUI screen layout changes).
Enterprise Software Scenario 2 (Taxpayer Z / Customer B)

Customer B contracts with Taxpayer Z to integrate Z's inventory software with a third-party real-time sensor array using a novel asynchronous communication protocol where data-parsing latency is uncertain, requiring redesign and testing of middleware architectures.
Qualified Research Overcoming Exclusion.

Conditionally Qualified: Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3), customer specificity does not disqualify the work, and resolving middleware data-synchronization and latency uncertainties via systematic trial-and-error testing of alternative caching/parsing architectures aligns with 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 10. However, Taxpayer Z must substantiate that (1) at least 80% of the middleware subset's research activities constituted elements of a computer-science PoE (§ 1.41-4(a)(6) and § 1.41-4(b)(2)), and (2) the contract is not excluded funded research under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H).
Scenario Lab s1: UI Configuration
A client requests their corporate color scheme, logo, and rearranged dashboard widgets applied to an existing software platform using built-in settings or standard CSS.
Likely Excluded (Adaptation).

Excluded: Barred on three independent grounds: (1) 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii) (style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors, illustrated by § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 1); (2) 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3) (adaptation of an existing component without technical uncertainty); and (3) IRS Software PoE Audit Guidelines classifying GUI screen arrangement and Software application configuration as non-qualifying.
Scenario Lab s2: Legacy Integration Bridge

A client requires syncing a modern SaaS platform with an undocumented 1990s mainframe that uses an encrypted binary format, requiring engineers to reverse-engineer the binary format and build a novel data translation layer.
Likely Qualified.

Split / Mixed Audit Risk (Requires Shrinking Back): While designing and testing alternative architectures for a novel data-synchronization translation layer can qualify under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 10 and § 1.41-4(c)(3), the IRS Software PoE Audit Guidelines explicitly warn under Reverse engineering that "examining existing programs, databases, and files in order to figure out how an existing application really works" (specifically citing legacy interface reverse engineering) "is not qualified research under I.R.C. § 41(d). See Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 8." If reverse-engineering the legacy binary format consumes more than 20% of total project research activities, the overall integration bridge fails the 80% substantially all test (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6)), requiring the taxpayer to shrink back under § 1.41-4(b)(2) strictly to the novel translation algorithm.
Scenario Lab s3: Custom Report Generation
A client needs a new PDF report aggregating columns A, B, and F (which were never previously combined) using standard SQL queries and layout tools.
Likely Excluded (Adaptation).

Excluded: Excluded under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3), 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(7) (routine manipulation/processing of data using information technology), and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 9 (standard ERP report generation). Also explicitly listed under High-Risk Vendor product extensions ("develop software to customize the format of a report") in the IRS Software PoE Audit Guidelines.
Scenario Lab m1: Resizing Product Dimensions
A customer requests a standard mounting bracket lengthened by 10% to fit their assembly line, where existing material strength is known to be sufficient.
Likely Excluded (Adaptation).

Excluded: Directly analogous to 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 6 (passenger rail car modified with fewer seats and standard materials) and Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84 (site-specific dimensional/standard adjustments to an existing design where engineering calculations are known at the outset).
Scenario Lab m2: High-Temp Environment Adaptation

A customer needs a standard sensor (rated to 150°C) adapted to operate in a 500°C turbine environment where existing casing materials melt at 300°C, requiring formulation and testing of a new composite casing compound.
Likely Qualified.

Conditionally Qualified: Analogous to 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 7 (modifying robotic equipment through modeling, simulation, and laboratory testing of alternatives) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 3 (developing a fine-shred food blade from new materials because existing blade material breaks). Even if the internal sensor electronics remain unchanged, the taxpayer can apply the shrinking-back rule (26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)) to isolate the new high-temperature casing compound (a separate formula/material subcomponent), provided at least 80% of the casing research activities constitute a qualifying PoE (§ 1.41-4(a)(6)).

body.text: Audit Enforcement, Substantiation, and Refund Claim Currency
IRS Audit Focus and Regulatory Example Citations

While an earlier truncated webpage scrape omitted the adaptation subsection, full extraction of the official IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 — Qualified Research Activities (published June 2005, republished 2008, webpage updated July 2, 2026) confirms that Section 5 (Excluded Activities) contains Subsection 2. Exclusion for Adaptation, which instructs IRS examiners verbatim as follows:

2. Exclusion for Adaptation This exclusion applies if the taxpayer's activities relate to adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need. This exclusion does not apply merely because a business component is intended for a specific customer. A contractor's adaptation of an existing business component to a taxpayer's particular requirement or need is not qualified research. Treasury Regulation section 1.41-4(c)(10), Examples 3-7, illustrates the application of the adaptation exclusion.

In parallel, the IRS Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software (updated June 8, 2026)—which focuses specifically on computer software examinations—contains the identical three-sentence explanation under Section "2. Selected exclusions from qualified research — Exclusion for adaptation," but narrows the regulatory example citation to software and equipment modification: "Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(10), Examples 3 and 7, illustrate the application of the adaptation exclusion."
Across the full text of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10) (Illustrations), the ten regulatory examples map to the IRC § 41(d)(4) statutory exclusions as follows:

items: Examples 1 and 2 (Research After Commercial Production): Illustrate the exclusion for research after commercial production under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2) (for instance, Example 1 contrasts qualifying engineering tests to design a novel cooling belt for tire manufacturing with excluded post-development costs to manufacture, install, and test the belts in commercial production).

Examples 3, 4, and 5 (Software Adaptation Across Vendor and Customer): Illustrate the adaptation exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3) where software development firm X adapts a core general ledger accounting software program to the specific requirements of customer C—disallowing X's in-house adaptation costs (Example 3), C's contract research payments to X (Example 4), and C's in-house employee wages when C's own staff adapts the program (Example 5).

Example 6 (Passenger Rail Car Adaptation): Illustrates the adaptation exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3) in manufacturing, where rail car manufacturer X fulfills an order from customer B for passenger rail cars differing from existing models solely by having fewer seats and commercially available upgraded seating material and carpet.

Example 7 (Robotic Equipment Modification Overcoming Adaptation): Illustrates overcoming the adaptation exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3) where valve manufacturer X purchases preexisting robotic equipment and conducts modeling, simulation, and extensive scientific and laboratory testing of alternative designs to resolve technological uncertainty on how to modify the robotic equipment for a new valve manufacturing process. (Note: A separate Example 7 under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8) addresses round-robin web-server load balancing under the process of experimentation rules, and another Example 7 under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(viii) addresses third-party website software under the internal-use software rules.)

Example 8 (Duplication Versus Alternative Formulation Experimentation): Illustrates the duplication exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4) (and is cited by the IRS Software PoE Audit Guidelines against reverse engineering), where X analyzes and reproduces ingredients A and B of competitor Y's gasoline additive (excluded duplication), but then conducts a qualifying process of experimentation to develop and test alternative lower-cost replacements for ingredient C (not excluded as duplication).

Example 9 (Management Functions and Organizational Restructuring): Illustrates the exclusion for surveys, studies, and management functions under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5), where manufacturing corporation X hires management consultants to interview employees and restructure its manufacturing organization.

Example 10 (Social Sciences and Actuarial/Pricing Research): Illustrates the exclusion for social sciences, arts, or humanities under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(8), where insurance company X researches pricing demand elasticity, tax consequences, interest rate volatility, and mortality tables for a new life insurance product.

body.text: Substantiation Strategy and Post-2021 Refund Claim Updates

Both the general IRS Research Credit ATG and the IRS Software PoE Audit Guidelines emphasize that the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of establishing that all requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1) have been satisfied for each claimed business component. Specifically, the general ATG directs examiners to issue an Information Document Request (IDR) at the outset of an examination requesting a complete list of each qualifying project or activity, a complete technical description of the activity, and the specific business component to which each research activity relates, supplemented by employee interviews to corroborate contemporaneous records. As demonstrated in Betz v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2023-84) and Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner (62 F.4th 287), taxpayers performing custom contract work who rely solely on customer proposals, final production drawings, or retrospective oral testimony face disallowance.

First, issued by the Office of Chief Counsel on September 17, 2021, and released to the public on October 15, 2021 (Memorandum Number 20214101F, Control Number POSTS-104459-20, UILC 6402.04-00, 6402.04-02, 41.00-00), the memorandum interprets the regulatory specificity requirement of Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1) in the context of IRC § 41 administrative refund claims filed within the IRC § 6511 statutory limitations period (3 years from return filing or 2 years from tax payment). Under Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1), a valid claim for refund or credit "must set forth in detail each ground upon which a credit or refund is claimed and facts sufficient to apprise the Commissioner of the exact basis thereof," verified by a written declaration signed under penalties of perjury; a claim that fails to comply "will not be considered for any purpose as a claim for refund or credit" and fails to confer subject-matter jurisdiction on a federal court under IRC § 7422(a) (absent an IRS waiver on the merits, as occurred in Harper v. United States, 2021 WL 732970 (9th Cir. Feb. 25, 2021)). Relying on Supreme Court and circuit precedent (United States v. Felt & Tarrant Mfg. Co., 283 U.S. 269 (1931); United States v. Memphis Cotton Oil Co., 288 U.S. 62 (1933); Angelus Milling Co. v. Commissioner, 325 U.S. 293 (1945); Stoller v. United States, 444 F.2d 1391 (5th Cir. 1971); and Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000)), CCM 20214101F originally required taxpayers filing an administrative refund claim starting January 10, 2022, to provide five items of factual information at filing: (1) identify all the business components (IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)) to which the IRC § 41 research credit claim relates for that claim year; (2) for each business component, identify all research activities performed; (3) for each business component, identify all individuals who performed each research activity; (4) for each business component, identify all the information each individual sought to discover; and (5) provide the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year (which may be provided via Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities), accompanied by a declaration signed under penalties of perjury and exact page citations if a multi-page credit study is attached.

Second, subsequent IRS administrative guidance significantly streamlined the upfront filing burden. Under Large Business and International (LB&I) directive LB&I-04-0125-0001 (dated January 3, 2025, effective for claims filed on or after January 10, 2022, expiring January 3, 2027, and updating Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) 4.46.3, IRM 4.10.11, and IRM 4.1.1 to supersede LB&I-04-1222-0026), the IRS confirmed that effective for refund claims postmarked as of June 18, 2024, the Service waived the upfront requirement to provide the names of the individuals who performed each research activity and the information each individual sought to discover at the time the refund claim is filed. Consequently, for Research Credit refund claims postmarked on or after June 18, 2024, taxpayers must provide three factual items plus the perjury declaration at filing:

items: Identification of Business Components: Identify all IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) business components that form the factual basis of the research credit claim for the claim year.

Description of Research Activities by Business Component: Identify all research activities performed by business component, including a description of what the taxpayer did and how they did it, by business component (language that simply restates the statutory or regulatory text of IRC § 41(d)(1) is explicitly rejected as insufficient).

Total Qualified Expenses and Perjury Declaration: Provide the total amounts of qualified employee wage expenses, qualified supply expenses, and qualified contract research expenses for the claim year (satisfied by a properly completed Form 6765), accompanied by a declaration signed under penalties of perjury verifying that the facts provided are accurate.

body.text: However, LB&I-04-0125-0001 and FAQ 10 on the IRS Research Credit Claims (Section 41) on Amended Returns Frequently Asked Questions page (updated October 1, 2026) emphasize that if a refund claim is selected for examination, examiners may still request the names (or specific titles/positions and headcount) of the individuals who performed the research activities and the specific information each sought to discover.

Third, the transition period during which taxpayers are afforded 45 days to perfect a deficient Research Credit refund claim has been extended twice beyond its initial January 10, 2022–January 9, 2024 window. While LB&I-04-0125-0001 reflected an earlier November 25, 2024 announcement extending the transition period through January 10, 2026, subsequent Taxpayer Services interim guidance TS-21-0126-0032 (dated January 2, 2026, updating IRM 21.7.4.4.8.3.5(16)) and the IRS Amended Returns FAQ page (updated October 1, 2026) confirm that the 45-day perfection period now extends through January 10, 2027 for Research Credit refund claims filed on Forms 1120X, 1040X, and amended Forms 1041 between January 10, 2022, and January 10, 2027. Under TS-21-0126-0032 and the IRS FAQs, if a claim lacks required information, Accounts Management (AM) or Campus personnel issue Letter 6426C, Letter 6428, or Letter 916C notifying the taxpayer of the deficiency and granting 45 days to respond (by fax or mail; portable electronic storage devices such as USB drives are rejected under FAQ 9). If the taxpayer responds, the case is re-suspended to CAT-A for classifier evaluation; if no response is received within 60 days (or if the perfection submission remains deficient), AM issues Letter 6424C - No Consider rejecting the claim. Pass-through entities must likewise comply (BBA partnerships via an Administrative Adjustment Request with Forms 8985/8986, and non-BBA pass-through entities and their partners/shareholders via amended return attachments under FAQ 13), and C corporations filing Form 1120 remain barred from filing informal Research Credit refund claims under Notice 2008-39 (FAQ 17).

Fourth, primary review of CCM 20214101F confirms that the memorandum addresses only administrative claims for refund or credit (not credits claimed on original timely filed returns) and never mentions the IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) adaptation exclusion.
Assessment of Policy Recommendations

None of these three recommendations represents enacted federal tax law, current Treasury regulations, or pending IRS administrative guidance; rather, each is a normative policy proposal originating outside government that must be evaluated against existing law.

cells: Recommendation 1: Regulatory Decision Tree in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3)

Amend 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3) to incorporate a binding, multi-step decision tree establishing that customer-driven R&D is "presumptively qualified" whenever the taxpayer resolves scientific or engineering uncertainties through a documented process of experimentation.
Normative proposal only (not enacted law or pending Treasury regulation).

Partially Aligned in Concept, Conflicting on Burden of Proof: The preamble to T.D. 9104 already states Treasury's view that IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) does not exclude activities that otherwise satisfy IRC § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a). However, creating a regulatory presumption of qualification would conflict with T.D. 9104, the IRS ATGs, and Seventh Circuit precedent in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner (62 F.4th 287), all of which place the affirmative burden of proving every element of IRC § 41(d)(1) and the 80% fraction under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) squarely on the taxpayer.
Recommendation 2: Modernized Revenue Ruling or Updated ATG Examples

Issue a binding Revenue Ruling or updated ATG providing at least five contemporary examples—specifically contrasting excluded "customization of data sets" with novel data parsing/integration—to modernize 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Examples 3 and 7.
Normative proposal only (not current IRS guidance).

Substantively Sound Observation: In the preamble to T.D. 9104, Treasury and the IRS stated that the multitude of factual situations to which the commercial production, adaptation, and duplication exclusions apply made additional broad regulatory rules impractical. While Examples 3–7 of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10) (covering general ledger software, passenger rail cars, and valve robotics) date to 2004, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Examples 9 and 10 and the IRS Software PoE Audit Guidelines already contrast non-qualifying ERP data conversion/report configuration with qualifying trial-and-error development of novel data-caching and synchronization algorithms.
Recommendation 3: Mandatory Pre-Project Technical Uncertainty Assessment Report

Require all taxpayers claiming credits for customer-contract research to generate and maintain a pre-dated "Technical Uncertainty Assessment Report" prior to commencing work, formally documenting the existing component, the technical unknowns, and the planned evaluation of alternatives.
Normative proposal only (not an IRS statutory or regulatory mandate).

Exceeds Regulatory Recordkeeping Rules (26 CFR § 1.41-4(d)): Although 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) and Betz v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2023-84) require that technical uncertainty exist "as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities," T.D. 9104 adopted flexible recordkeeping rules in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) after taxpayers objected to rigid documentation mandates in the 2001 regulations (T.D. 8930 and Notice 2001-19). Mandating a single pre-project form would penalize taxpayers whose contemporaneous engineering records are generated iteratively in native project tools.

body.text: At the same time, existing Treasury regulations and judicial precedent already provide a coherent analytical path: customer specificity does not disqualify a project per se under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3), and taxpayers who maintain granular, subcomponent-level documentation of their upfront design uncertainties, alternative evaluations, and 80% experimentation allocation can substantiate custom development work under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6) and (b)(2).
